title: Happy birthday to the dean, the 411 on 311 on 3/11, and a standing invitation, in political notes
summary: House and Senate take a minute to wish a happy 85th birthday to Sen. Joanne C. Benson, Sen. Cheryl Kagan talks 311 on 3/11, and the Black Caucus tells Environment Secretary Serena McIlwain don't be a stranger, in political notes.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters March 12, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters March 12, 2026

Legislators in both chambers paid homage this week to one of the General Assembly’s longest-serving members, Sen. Joanne C. Benson (D-Prince George’s), who turned 85 on Wednesday.

Benson was not on hand to see her colleagues stand and applaud her, because she has not been present in the Senate since the 90-day session began Jan. 14. But the senator, affectionately called “the dean” of the Senate and currently the chamber’s majority whip, remains admired by her colleagues.

Sen. Ron Watson (D-Prince George’s) read prepared remarks summarizing her 35 years in the General Assembly, including 20 years in the House.

“She has been a powerful voice for education equity and opportunity dedicating her life to uplifting communities and expanding access to resources for those who need them most,” Watson said. “Her legacy is one of courage, commitment and community. Sen. Benson has shown us what it means to lead with purpose and to serve with integrity.”

Benson, who represents the county’s 24th legislative district, was not only the second woman to chair the state’s Legislative Black Caucus, now more than 60 members strong, but she also ensured the caucus had an office that represents an “institutional home” in the House of Delegates building.

Across the hall in the House chambers, Del. Tiffany Alston (D-Prince George’s) wished Benson a happy birthday for herself and her 24th District colleagues, Dels. Andrea Fletcher Harrison and Derrick Coley.

“Please give her a virtual hug,” Alston said. “And as she always likes to say, ‘We love her a bushel and peck and a hug around the neck.’ Happy birthday, Sen. Benson.”

With Benson not seeking reelection, two people have filed to run for her seat in the June 23 Democratic primary: Alston and real estate broker Kevin Ford Jr.

When she designated Wednesday as 3-1-1 Day, Sen. Cheryl Kagan (D-Montgomery) was not merely referencing the date, March 11.

She was referencing the fact that her bill to create a statewide, nonemergency phone system passed a preliminary vote and was headed toward final approval on the Senate floor. Senate Bill 114, a passion project for Kagan, also seeks to use artificial intelligence to answer callers’ questions and report minor incidents such as library closings, dates and times for early voting, or places to get a flu shot.

The main goal: Decrease the number of calls to 911. If approved, Maryland would be the first state in the nation with a statewide system.

The legislation stems from a November report by a work group that unanimously recommended the state create a phased approach to implementing a 311 system statewide, beginning with systems in four counties using artificial intelligence chatbots, ultimately expanding to a statewide system employing AI voice bots.

The bill’s fiscal note estimates at least $1 million would be needed in fiscal 2027 to hire a program manager, county liaison and a data specialist; conduct a media campaign to advertise the program; and coordinate with participating counties to ensure the chatbot and voicebot provide accurate information. The note also highlights that the network estimates “the need for similar annual funding levels through fiscal 2031 to administer and expand the 3-1-1 program.”

Cost savings would be realized because of assistance from the Maryland Information Network (MDInfoNet), which already manages statewide social service referrals through a 211 system. A 311 oversight board would be created within the information network.

Baltimore City and Anne Arundel, Baltimore, Montgomery, Prince George’s and St. Mary’s counties already operate a 311 system. An AI chatbot would be rolled out in two counties with a 311 system and another two without one. By June 30, 2027, a chatbot would be established in each county to include multilingual support, integration with geographic information system data and “clear escalation protocols to route complex requests to live agents.” The bill says a county “may choose not to participate” in the 311 program by submitting a letter to the board within 14 days after stating the reason why.

“This is going to supplement, not supplant where it exists now,” said Kagan, who has worked on this for seven years. “The counties, we give them flexibility as to how, when and whether to engage with this, but they will be part of the interoperability.”

A House version of the bill, sponsored by Del. Lesley Lopez (D-Montgomery), had a hearing last month. It has not yet come up for a vote.

Environment Secretary Serena McIlwain visited the Legislative Black Caucus Thursday to make a pitch for House Bill 1268 and Senate Bill 781, the Cumulative Harms for Environmental Restoration for Improving Shared Health, or CHERISH Our Communities Act.

A hearing on the Senate version, sponsored by Sen. Benjamin Brooks (D-Baltimore County), was held March 3 before the Education, Energy and the Environment Committee. The Environment and Transportation Committee is scheduled to review the House version Friday. A similar bill died last year.

“This bill will allow us to look at these permits differently. Look at the environmental scores in those areas and put a little more pressure … on making sure you’re mitigating pollution,” McIlwain said. “I hope that we can get this bill passed so I can sleep. It’s been up for four years.”

She received support from the caucus, but also slight criticism from Sen. Antonio Hayes (D-Baltimore City), who said she doesn’t have “to wait for an invitation” to stand with the Black Caucus. “I would love to see you just be out there, more visible because the stuff that you’re doing is visionary. There’s not many places in this country that are doing the type of stuff that you’re doing,” Hayes said.

“I’m happy to know that I don’t need an invitation and I can just start being a part of this wonderful group,” McIlwain said. “I’ll step it up.”

Del. N. Scott Phillips (D-Baltimore County), chair of the caucus, said the CHERISH Act is on the priority agenda for the caucus, which will “do what we can to get it across.”

Phillips on Thursday also presented an encased glass gavel to Del. Jheanelle Wilkins (D-Montgomery) for her service as the caucus chair between December 2022 through January of this year.

“Don’t hurt anybody with it,” Phillips joked. “Thank you for everything you did in leading us. Hopefully something that you will be able to lay on your desk and remember your time as the chair of the Legislative Black Caucus.”
